newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - YAMAICHI OUSTS TOP BRASS, BUT HURDLES REMAIN.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - YAMAICHI OUSTS TOP BRASS, BUT HURDLES REMAIN.

text.p: Yamaichi Securities, one of Japan's biggest financial firms, went through a corporate bloodletting on Monday to shake off the effects of a racketeer scandal, but analysts said its new leaders still face troubles ahead.
Yamaichi announced that its chairman, president and five vice presidents were resigning to take responsibility for the scandal.
Four other executives resigned as part of the firm's efforts to restructure its management in response to Japan's "Big Bang" financial deregulations.
The shake-up at what is the smallest and weakest of Japan's four biggest brokerages, was widely expected after prosecutors raided the company and the homes of its top executives last month.
Senior managing director Shoji Saotome replaced chairman Tsugio Yukihira and senior managing director Shohei Nozawa succeeded president Atsuo Miki.

"Our firm is determined to make a clean break with the negative legacy of the past," Nozawa said, in a refrain heard in recent weeks from executives at other financial firms tainted by the scandal involving payoffs to a corporate racketeer.

The so-called "sokaiya" racketeers buy shares in companies and try to extort money from them by threatening to expose dubious business practices. Payoffs to sokaiya have been illegal since 1983, but many firms have found it tough to cut off ties to the underworld.

Yamaichi is suspected of making 79 million yen ($686,000) in illegal payoffs in 1995 to Ryuichi Koike, the sokaiya at the heart of the scandal that has also ensnared Nomura Securities Co and Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB).

Analysts said that compared with a sweeping management shake-up announced by giant Nomura in late April, Yamaichi's selection of senior managing directors, both 59 years old, to replace the chairman and president did not impress.

"Compared with Nomura's reshuffle, Yamaichi's action is not so impressive...It looks like the new management will only pursue strategies already decided by former leaders," said an analyst at a foreign securities house.
In April, Nomura surprised the financial markets by announcing that 51-year-old Junichi Ujiie would take over on May 1 as president of what is Japan's biggest brokerage.
Ujiie is seen as the type of young, untainted leader with wide international experience that Nomura needs to help win back public trust.
Ayako Sato, an analyst at UBS Securities, said she would wait for the management policy of the new Yamaichi leadership to emerge before assessing the firm's future performance.
However, she said that if it took some time for prosecutors to complete their probe, it would hurt the firm's bottom-line severely.

Indeed, Shoji Saotome, who replaced Tsugio Yukihira as chairman effective Monday, told reporters that Yamaichi's alleged involvement in the scandal had already hurt its business. He said that after prosecutors raided Yamaichi offices in July, two corporations had asked the brokerage to withdraw from the underwriting syndicate for their bonds.

Even without the scandal, Yamaichi faces a hard time securing its position amid financial deregulation, including liberalisation of commissions from stock-broking business and banks' entry into the market.

In the April-June period, when corporate customers voluntarily suspended their securities business with Nomura, Yamaichi failed to attract new domestic customers and posted 5.43 billion yen ($47.2 million) in parent current losses.
Some analysts believe Yamaichi may be obliged to form an alliance with a foreign firm or to team up with a bank to survive in the "Big Bang" reforms.

Last month, Yamaichi said it would streamline its corporate structure and operations in European and American markets to correct its high-cost structure. Last month it also started reducing salaries of company executives by 10 to 25 percent. ($1=115 yen)
